thread.title_full: Trump: US and Iran will talk next week, nuclear sites 'obliterated' - NewsBreak

author: DPA
title: Trump: US and Iran will talk next week, nuclear sites 'obliterated' - NewsBreak
text: US President Donald Trump said he expects talks with Iran to take place "next week," following what he called the end of the war between Israel and Iran and the "total obliteration" of Iran's nuclear facilities by US airstrikes. Speaking at the NATO summit in The Hague on Wednesday, Trump said Israel and Iran "fought a hell of a war," but that it ended when US forces attacked Iranian sites last weekend. Trump repeatedly expressed his disdain over US media reports citing intelligence officials suggesting the attacks may have not damaged the Iranian nuclear programme to the extent claimed by his administration. "I think it was total obliteration," he said, adding that he did not agree with claims that Iran moved its enriched uranium out of the sites prior to the US strikes using bunker-busting bombs. "I believe they didn't have a chance to get anything out, because we acted fast." At the summit's closing press conference, he said the nuclear materials were likely "covered with granite, concrete and steel" due to the blasts. Damage assessments disputed The past 24 hours have seen a swirl of differing information about the actual impact of the ambitious US strikes on the three nuclear facilities at Isfahan, Natanz and Fordow. An initial intelligence evaluation suggested that the bombardment had set back Iran's nuclear programme by only a few months, The New York Times, The Washington Post and CNN reported on Tuesday, citing officials familiar with a military intelligence report from the Pentagon's Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA). Trump soon afterwards blasted the media reports as "fake news" and maintained that Iran's nuclear programme had been hindered "basically decades." He went further at the NATO summit on Wednesday, saying that CNN, MSNBC and The New York Times were "scum" for their reporting on the issue. The Israeli military said on Wednesday that it believed the attacks had set back the Iranian nuclear programme by years, but it was too early to be certain of this. The current military assessment is that it was badly damaged, said military spokesman Effie Defrin. Diplomacy ahead? Trump said in The Hague, where he spent two days meeting with fellow leaders of NATO countries, that talks with Iran were imminent. "We're going to talk to them next week," he said, adding that the two countries "may sign an agreement." He went on: "I don't care if I have an agreement or not. The only thing we'd be asking for is what we were asking for before. We want no nuclear. But we destroyed the nuclear." Tensions have soared since June 13, when Israel launched a large-scale bombardment of Iranian military and nuclear infrastructure, killing several top officials. In response, Iran conducted direct missile strikes on Israeli territory. Last weekend, Trump ordered a US attack on Iranian nuclear targets. Israel and Iran agreed to a ceasefire that went into effect on Tuesday and which has largely held. Iran confirms death of senior commander Iran on Wednesday confirmed the death of Major General Ali Shadmani, a senior commander in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, following an Israeli airstrike last week. The state-affiliated Fars news agency reported that Shadmani succumbed to injuries sustained in the attack. Israel's military had announced Shadmani's death last week, calling him the "highest-ranking military commander" killed in the war. However, Iranian officials had not issued any confirmation until now. Shadmani served as the commander of the central headquarters Khatam-al Anbiya, a key operational division of the Revolutionary Guards under the General Staff. He succeeded Gholam Ali Rashid, who was killed in an Israeli strike at the onset of the war. According to Israel, more than 20 high-ranking Iranian military officials were killed in Israeli airstrikes. Israeli attacks on Iran killed at least 627 people and injured 4,870, according to Iran's Health Ministry, with most fatalities in Tehran. The US-based rights group HRANA put the death toll at over 1,000, citing informants and public sources over the 12-day conflict. In Israel, 29 people were killed and hundreds more wounded by Iranian attacks. Israeli intelligence to remain active in Iran Mossad chief David Barnea said on Wednesday that Israel's foreign intelligence service will continue operating inside Iran. In a rare video appearance, Barnea addressed Mossad agents. "We will be there, just as we have been there until now," he said, referring to operations on Iranian soil. Barnea credited Mossad's actions with helping Israel achieve wartime objectives that "previously seemed unrealistic." The large-scale Israeli strikes on Iran were reportedly coordinated by Mossad, with support from operatives embedded deep within Iranian territory. These agents are said to have deployed and operated precision weapons and drones from inside the country, targeting air defence systems and missile silos in central Iran. During the conflict, Iranian authorities carried out a wave of arrests, detaining several individuals accused of spying for Mossad.
